title: Pitching: capacity, execution and exposure
subtitle: Four decisions that connect physical preparation with the actual pitching task.
context:
You join a synthetic professional development staff at the end of a training block. The athlete's gym results, bullpen observations and throwing records point in different directions. Your role is to help the team ask better questions and select the next useful action.

Work through a capacity review, a pitch-mix audit, a video discussion and a throwing-exposure handoff. Each episode changes the information available. Numbers are supplied so you can check the conclusion yourself; they are not professional benchmarks.
outcomes: Separate a physical-capacity gain from baseball transfer and causal explanation.
Audit pitch-type composition, measurement context and incomplete throwing records.
Write a practical handoff with a next action, an owner and a visible uncertainty.
scope: All players, schedules, observations and numerical values are synthetic teaching examples. These decisions practice interpretation and coordination, not medical clearance, a validated injury-prediction system or an experimentally optimal training plan.

links.label: Choose a test for the baseball question

stages.title: Strength increased. Did pitching improve?
stages.brief: A healthy synthetic professional starting pitcher finishes a six-week development block. A standardized trap-bar test rises from 180 to 192 kg. His mean four-seam velocity in two matched, coach-supervised bullpens changes from 92.0 to 92.1 mph; target-hit counts are 13/20 and 14/20. The number of observations is small and local error estimates are unavailable. The pitching coach asks whether the strength block failed.

teaching.heading: Separate capacity, execution and outcome
teaching.text:
A physical-capacity test asks what the athlete can produce within that test's constraints. A throwing task asks how the athlete coordinates a different action, at different speeds, with a ball and a target. A competitive result introduces still more influences. These are linked questions, but they are not interchangeable measurements. An improved lift is evidence about that lift before it is evidence about pitching.

Build three columns: the physical quality targeted, the baseball behavior expected to benefit, and the observation that would make you reconsider. Here the first column improved. The second is unresolved. A sensible next step is to inspect whether the original development target was actually a plausible limiting factor, while retaining the new capacity if it remains useful and affordable.

teaching.heading: Write a claim that matches the design
teaching.text:
The lift increased by 12 kg, or 6.7% relative to 180 kg. The velocity difference is 0.1 mph; without a local error estimate and repeated matched sessions, that number should not be sold as adaptation. Target hits changed by one successful pitch. Neither result identifies a muscle, a mechanical fault or a causal effect of the training block.

Ask the athlete how the training fit throwing preparation and review adherence, pitch intent, equipment and test timing. The conversation can support a modified next block without forcing a verdict of success or failure on every outcome. Predefine when the staff will review the next matched observations rather than chasing the best single pitch.

decision.prompt: What is the most defensible response to the pitching coach?

options.text: Keep the strength gain, verify the baseball outcome over repeated matched sessions, and revisit the original limiting-factor hypothesis.
options.feedback: Best answer. This acknowledges a measured capacity gain without claiming transfer, then makes the next review useful.

options.text: Replace the strength block immediately with only high-speed work because velocity did not rise.
options.feedback: The new emphasis might eventually be justified, but two bullpen summaries do not establish that strength work failed or that high-speed work is the missing cause.

options.text: Repeat the same block unchanged because the larger lift guarantees delayed velocity transfer.
options.feedback: The lift improved, but neither a guaranteed transfer nor a predictable delay follows from these observations.

worked: Report: “The strength-test result improved 6.7%. We have not established a meaningful change in bullpen velocity or execution. The next review will use the same pitch type, device, intent and session context, alongside the pitching coach’s task observations.”

stages.title: A faster average can hide slower pitches
stages.brief: Session A contains 20 four-seam pitches averaging 92 mph and 10 changeups averaging 84 mph. Session B contains 25 four-seam pitches averaging 91 mph and five changeups averaging 83 mph. Both sessions have 30 tracked pitches. A dashboard pools pitch types and announces “velocity improved.” These are synthetic arithmetic examples, not player norms.

teaching.heading: Check the denominator before the story
teaching.text:
The pooled average in A is (20 × 92 + 10 × 84) / 30 = 89.33 mph. In B it is (25 × 91 + 5 × 83) / 30 = 89.67 mph. The pooled result rises by 0.33 mph even though each pitch-type mean is 1 mph lower. More of the faster pitch type entered the second sample. This is a composition effect, not a contradiction.

For a pitching development question, compare like with like: pitch classification, intended task, device, mound setting, session phase and observation count. Keep the all-pitch number if operations needs it, but label its purpose. An aggregate can answer “what was thrown today?” while failing to answer “did this pitch improve?”

teaching.heading: Separate delivery of the task from selection of the task
teaching.text:
A pitcher may change pitch mix for a planned tactical reason. That decision is not a training failure. It does mean the analyst must separate within-pitch changes from changing opportunities. Missing velocity readings also need a count; quietly dropping untracked throws can change the apparent distribution.

The staff report should show both the type-specific summary and its denominator. It should also preserve location or execution measures rather than use speed as the whole definition of pitch quality. These means alone do not measure pitch movement, deception, command or tissue loading. The next action is an interpretation review, not a biomechanical diagnosis from a spreadsheet.

stages.title: Video identifies a question, not a joint load
stages.brief: The coach reviews ordinary side-view video and notices a different stride pattern on several pitches. The athlete reports trying a new cue. No calibrated three-dimensional capture, force data, synchronized timing validation or joint-load model is available. A colleague proposes prescribing a specific hip exercise because the pitcher looks “late.”

teaching.heading: Use observation to narrow the next question
teaching.text:
A video clip can support a conversation about what visibly changed, when it occurred and whether the intended task was performed. Document camera position, frame rate, the event being compared and which pitches were selected. A side view compresses movement into a projection. Rotation outside that plane, camera movement and event selection can alter the apparent picture.

First ask the pitching coach what “late” means in observable task language. It might refer to a release event relative to another event, a missed location or a subjective impression. Those meanings call for different observations. Do not turn an ambiguous label into a measured timing deficit simply because a freeze-frame looks persuasive.

teaching.heading: Match the claim to the instrument and owner
teaching.text:
An exercise choice can be based on a documented physical need and a reasonable training hypothesis. It is not proof that the selected exercise will repair a delivery pattern. Likewise, ordinary video does not directly measure internal elbow torque, ligament strain or a particular muscle's contribution. Those claims require suitable methods, assumptions and relevant expertise.

Pair the pitching coach's task question with the S&C coach's capacity assessment and the analyst's measurement plan. If the video suggests a clinical concern, the medical team determines that assessment. The immediate nonclinical output here is a short observation protocol: what to film again, which comparable pitches to include, and what would count as an informative change.

stages.title: The game total is only one exposure record
stages.brief: A synthetic outing log contains 72 game pitches, 22 pregame bullpen pitches and 30 between-inning pitches. Catch play is recorded as “completed” with no throw count. The next day's lift is due for review. The athlete reports ordinary baseline soreness, but no clinician has made a new readiness assessment. The numbers describe recorded tasks; they do not carry validated recovery equivalents.

teaching.heading: Build an exposure ledger before a readiness score
teaching.text:
The observed categories total 124 counted throws: 72 + 22 + 30. The 52 counted throws outside the official game total are useful context. Catch play remains an unknown quantity, not zero. Retain purpose, surface, distance, intent description, sequencing and any available athlete response beside the count. Counting accurately improves the conversation even when it cannot quantify tissue stress.

A high-school observational study counted substantial mound work outside official game totals. That supports asking where the missing work is, not borrowing a professional recovery limit. This synthetic ledger is an operational example. It does not claim that 124 mixed throws equal 124 game pitches or that two throws with equal speed impose equal internal loading.

sourceRefs.locator: Methods and Results, pp. 1–3; limitations, p. 5: high-school outings and uncounted mound throws.

teaching.heading: Make the next session adjustable
teaching.text:
Review the planned lift against the intended adaptation, the next throwing task, the athlete's response and the staff's current assessment. A short maintenance option, a relocated session or the original plan may each be defensible depending on information that the count cannot provide. State what you would change and why; avoid pretending one arithmetic total selects the correct dose.

Assign someone to improve the catch-play record prospectively. Keep changes feasible: a shared log with task categories may be more useful than a precise-looking score built from guessed conversions. If the player develops unexpected symptoms, the decision pathway changes to clinical review. A stable jump result or a low official pitch count cannot independently clear the athlete.

title: Hitting and baserunning: test the right task
subtitle: Compare swing protocols, contact distributions and the journey to first base.
context:
You support a synthetic corner outfielder during a development block that must fit a competitive schedule. The hitting coach wants better contact quality and the baserunning coach wants a more effective first movement. The athlete also needs a sustainable strength plan.

The case deliberately supplies measurements that sound similar but describe different tasks. Your job is to preserve useful observations, correct misleading comparisons and allocate a small amount of preparation time to questions that matter.
outcomes: Define a reproducible bat-speed protocol and keep local tests distinct from game statistics.
Interpret contact distributions with explicit denominators and missing observations.
Connect controlled acceleration testing with baseball start transitions and feasible training.
scope: All players, schedules, observations and numerical values are synthetic teaching examples. These decisions practice interpretation and coordination, not medical clearance, a validated injury-prediction system or an experimentally optimal training plan.

stages.title: A bat-speed number needs a protocol
stages.brief: A synthetic corner outfielder performs two hitting assessments. Test A uses the same game bat against a fixed machine setting; ten valid swings average 70 mph on a local sensor. Test B uses a lighter training bat in dry swings; the selected five fastest swings average 74 mph. A staff note calls the difference a four-mph gain in game bat speed.

teaching.heading: Ask what actually moved and what was averaged
teaching.text:
The object, task, instrument and summary changed simultaneously. A local sensor's bat-speed estimate also needs a measurement-point definition. The same word on two dashboards does not establish the same measurement. Keep device version, sensor placement, bat properties, pitch delivery, intent, exclusions and the aggregation rule in the test record.

The official Statcast bat-tracking page specifies a bat location and a competitive-swing selection rule. Its main definition is more detailed than the shorthand in its footer. The local all-valid-swings mean in this case is deliberately a different protocol. Compare it with itself when evaluating a block; do not silently treat it as the published seasonal statistic.

sourceRefs.locator: Bat Tracking Leaderboard: introductory metric definitions and glossary; checked October 13, 2026.

teaching.heading: Choose the next comparison from the decision
teaching.text:
If the question concerns game-bat swing performance under a repeatable machine task, repeat Test A. If the question concerns a training-bat exercise, Test B may have its own useful record. Both can remain in the athlete's file, but they require separate names and interpretation. A faster selected sample with a different implement does not quantify adaptation in the original task.

Standardization need not eliminate every meaningful baseball variation. It creates a stable reference. Once the reference question is answered, the hitting coach can add varied pitch locations and speeds to examine execution. Label those tasks separately. The aim is to connect a controlled capacity observation with baseball behavior while preserving what each test can and cannot tell you.

stages.title: One hard contact is not the whole hitting profile
stages.brief: In a synthetic standardized machine session, ten tracked contacts in A have exit speeds of 88, 90, 91, 92, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97 and 104 mph. In B they are 90, 92, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97, 98, 99 and 101 mph. Each session also contains four swings without tracked contact. The hitting coach wants to know whether the athlete lost power because the best contact fell.

teaching.heading: Let the question select the summary
teaching.text:
The maximum fell from 104 to 101 mph. The mean of the ten tracked contacts rose from 94 to 95.5 mph. The median rose from 93.5 to 95.5 mph. These summaries are not competing versions of the truth: each answers a different question about the supplied sample. A peak asks about one observed ceiling; a mean or median describes the recorded distribution.

Do not select the statistic after seeing which one flatters the training plan. Predeclare the purpose and retain the individual observations. The four swings without tracked contact belong in the denominator audit, even though they have no exit-speed value to average. Record whether they were misses, fouls, failed tracking or another event; those categories answer different hitting questions.

teaching.heading: Connect the ball result with the task
teaching.text:
A ball's exit speed is an outcome of a contact event. It is not a direct measurement of the hitter's muscle power. To explain a change, the staff also needs task information such as pitch delivery, bat, contact conditions and execution. A sensor can report a number while leaving the explanation unresolved. The two synthetic ten-contact samples are too limited to establish stable game ability or a training effect.

Retain the standardized contact distribution and ask the hitting coach which additional execution observations matter. A useful review might examine whether a stable task is being performed more consistently while preserving the ability to produce strong contacts. Training decisions should follow that question, not automatically chase the single largest value at the expense of the rest of the session.

stages.title: Acceleration and top speed answer different questions
stages.brief: The same synthetic outfielder has a 10 m electronic-gate time of 1.88 s at baseline and 1.82 s at follow-up with a fixed start setup. A separate home-to-first video task remains 4.25 s. The staff also has a season-level game running-speed summary, but its qualifying opportunities and aggregation differ. No local test-retest error estimate has been completed.

teaching.heading: Preserve the start and the clock
teaching.text:
The 10 m time changed by −0.06 s, or a 3.2% time reduction relative to baseline. That is a descriptive result, not yet proof of meaningful adaptation. Gate height, first movement relative to the beam, stance, surface, footwear and timing rules can all change the interpretation. A standing sprint and a run that begins after a swing are different tasks.

Map the home-to-first sequence into leaving the box, accelerating and continuing toward the base. The official Baseball Savant teaching example illustrates why a sustained fastest-window statistic does not describe every earlier part of that sequence. It does not supply an intervention prescription or a universal threshold for this athlete.

sourceRefs.locator: A Story of Sprint Speed and Burst: Statcast Data and Components of Speed; historical 2017 illustration.

teaching.heading: Use matched physical and baseball observations
teaching.text:
The fixed-start sprint helps examine a repeatable physical task. The home-to-first task includes transition from the hitting action and its own timing rules. An unchanged total does not show which component stayed the same or offset another. Work with the baserunning and hitting coaches to observe the transition and running path; do not infer a leg-strength deficit from the total alone.

Choose a training target that the athlete can understand: for example, improve the consistency of an agreed box-exit task while retaining acceleration work that fits the weekly schedule. Then define how each task will be observed again. This links physical preparation with baseball execution without assuming a laboratory or field-test gain will automatically appear in competition.

stages.title: Allocate scarce time to an explicit baseball question
stages.brief: The next series permits two supervised 20-minute preparation windows. The athlete already has a hitting plan and usual team field work. You can preserve a short strength exposure, provide an acceleration practice, or collect a focused hitting assessment, but cannot fit every optional item. The standardized hitting and running results remain uncertain, and the next three games matter more than finishing a testing checklist.

teaching.heading: Choose the decision before adding the session
teaching.text:
Start with the next decision that could reasonably change the plan. If the staff needs to know whether a recent swing cue remains workable against varied delivery, that belongs with the hitting coach's practice. If it needs a repeatable acceleration observation, collect it within an appropriate running session. An extra generic test is not automatically the best use of limited preparation time.

A short maintenance exposure and a specific acceleration session may be defensible here, with the contact audit handled from existing records. Another allocation could be better if the athlete's current status or playing assignment changes. State the priority, what you defer and the cost of deferral. The case does not establish a universal twenty-minute program.

teaching.heading: Evaluate the plan across the actual baseball week
teaching.text:
The training dose includes more than the supervised window. Count scheduled running, swings and field repetitions by task, preserving unknowns. Coordinate timing so the athlete understands which session emphasizes development and which prepares the next task. The S&C practitioner should not independently rewrite the hitting program in order to improve a dashboard number.

Define a small review package: what was completed, the athlete's response, whether the intended baseball work remained available, and one matched observation when feasible. A plan that fits the week and generates interpretable feedback is more useful than an ambitious plan whose dose, purpose and consequences cannot be reconstructed.

title: Catching, fielding and the reserve role
subtitle: Keep timing, execution, duty records and unpredictable assignments connected.
context:
You support two synthetic players: a catcher working on a throwing cue and a utility reserve who sometimes catches and also plays the infield. Staff time is limited, duties vary and some practice records are incomplete. Neither player is currently in a prescribed rehabilitation pathway.

The case moves from a controlled throw sequence to a duty ledger, a fielding assessment and a travel-week plan. You must keep physical preparation useful without turning every measurement into a medical conclusion or every baseball drill into a complete test.
outcomes: Interpret the components of a catcher’s throw alongside target execution.
Record receiving, blocking and throwing without invented fatigue conversions.
Distinguish planned movement from fielding and build a revisable reserve plan.
scope: All players, schedules, observations and numerical values are synthetic teaching examples. These decisions practice interpretation and coordination, not medical clearance, a validated injury-prediction system or an experimentally optimal training plan.

stages.title: The catcher’s throw is a sequence
stages.brief: In a synthetic catcher drill, Protocol A averages 0.72 s from receipt to release and 1.36 s from release to the fixed receiving plane: 2.08 s total. A new cue produces 0.64 s plus 1.36 s: 2.00 s total. Eight of ten A throws enter the predeclared target zone, compared with five of ten under the new cue. Trial conditions and target geometry are unchanged.

teaching.heading: Decompose time without losing the task
teaching.text:
The new cue reduces the measured total by 0.08 s, entirely within the receipt-to-release interval in this example. That identifies where the observed difference occurred; it does not identify the muscular or technical cause. Keep the timestamp definitions and camera or sensor method fixed. A club's local receipt-to-plane task should be named as such rather than automatically labeled the official game metric.

Official Statcast documentation describes pop time using a projected receiving point at the base and distinguishes exchange from throw speed. The synthetic drill uses a fixed target-plane timing method. Its decomposition is useful locally, but official leaderboards are not interchangeable reference values for this custom task.

sourceRefs.locator: Pop Time Leaderboard: opening definition and exchange/throw metrics; checked October 13, 2026.

teaching.heading: Make speed and execution visible together
teaching.text:
The target-zone count fell from 80% to 50%: a 30 percentage-point difference. In ten trials per condition, that is three additional misses, not a stable estimate of future game performance. The staff cannot describe the faster total as an uncomplicated improvement while omitting the target result. Conversely, it should not declare the cue permanently ineffective from this small sample.

Discuss the drill's purpose with the catching coach. A constrained practice may intentionally explore a faster movement option before integrating accuracy, but the progression should say so. Record the cue, timing distribution, target result, pitch location and athlete response. The next assessment should examine whether the combination can be reproduced under the intended task constraints.

stages.title: Receiving, blocking and throwing need different records
stages.brief: A synthetic catcher completes two games in three days. The log records 165 pitches received, 11 blocked-ball events, eight competitive throws to bases and 35 pregame practice throws. Some receiving work in the bullpen is uncounted. The team asks for a single “catching load” score to select tomorrow's lower-body training dose.

teaching.heading: Describe the work before assigning weights
teaching.text:
These categories describe different tasks. Receiving a pitch is not one strength repetition; a block is not a validated equivalent number of squats; a throw to a base is not interchangeable with a pregame throw. Adding all categories as if they were equal creates a count with unclear meaning. Multiplying them by invented fatigue weights only hides the problem behind arithmetic.

Keep the categories alongside duration or innings, task intensity descriptions when available, surfaces, positions used and athlete response. This lets the staff ask practical questions: which duties were actually performed, which were absent from the record, and what is scheduled next? The athlete's own report complements the exposure ledger; neither is a stand-alone diagnosis.

teaching.heading: Support the next baseball task
teaching.text:
The next day's preparation must account for planned catching, hitting, running and strength work. Review whether a lower-body session serves a current development need and how it fits the athlete's response and schedule. A changed session can preserve useful training without treating a game count as an automatic prohibition or permission.

The receiving and blocking technique plan belongs with the catching staff, and symptom assessment belongs with the medical team. The S&C contribution includes physical preparation, dose organization and communication. A concise handoff names the next intended task, the known exposure categories and the missing bullpen record. That is more actionable than a red or green score whose weighting nobody can defend.

stages.title: A fast cone drill is not yet game fielding
stages.brief: The organization has a synthetic utility player who catches occasionally and also plays infield. His planned change-of-direction drill improves from 5.10 to 4.95 s under the same local timing protocol. In a separate coach-rated ground-ball drill, he completes the agreed field-and-throw task on six of ten randomized feeds before and after the block. Feed speed and difficulty were not standardized.

teaching.heading: Keep planned movement and perception separate
teaching.text:
The planned drill improved by 0.15 s, a 2.9% time reduction relative to baseline. The athlete knew the route in advance. A baseball fielding task also requires detecting the ball, selecting a route, arranging the body for the fielding action and executing a throw. A prescribed route can help train a component without measuring that whole sequence.

The strength-and-conditioning text distinguishes planned change of direction from agility that responds to a stimulus. Apply that distinction to the assessment label. Call the cone result a planned-drill result. Do not rename it “baseball agility improved” unless the additional task evidence supports that broader claim.

teaching.heading: Make the field task observable
teaching.text:
The unchanged six-of-ten count is difficult to interpret because the feeds differed. Preserve it as a practice observation, not a reliable performance test. With the infield coach, define the start position, feed categories, task success, timing events and sufficient repeatable opportunities. Keep representative uncertainty in skill practice, but identify which comparison is controlled enough to answer a measurement question.

A useful next block may combine physical braking or acceleration work with coach-led reactive fielding practice. The two components should have distinct purposes and review measures. A better cone time cannot establish superior perception, and a missed difficult feed cannot by itself diagnose insufficient strength. The plan should test the chosen explanation instead of assuming it.

stages.title: A reserve needs preparation for duties not yet performed
stages.brief: For the next road series, the utility player may catch one game, enter late as a defensive replacement and pinch-run. Over the previous week, he had little game action. Team practice logs are incomplete, so “no game sprints” does not mean “no sprint exposure.” There is one supervised preparation window before departure and uncertain access to the field afterward.

teaching.heading: Plan for plausible duties and actual recent work
teaching.text:
A reserve's immediate need is to remain prepared for an unpredictable assignment while continuing development when opportunity allows. Start by confirming recent practice, current athlete response, the likely duties and available facilities. A low game count is not evidence of complete recovery, nor proof that the player requires a large compensatory workout.

Create a short menu that preserves the qualities needed for likely tasks: an appropriate acceleration opportunity, a feasible strength exposure and coordinated fielding or catching practice. The exact dose depends on the athlete's established program and response. These are categories for planning, not a universal reserve prescription or a claim that every duty should be rehearsed maximally before travel.

teaching.heading: Use a trigger, an owner and a review
teaching.text:
Specify which change in assignment will alter the menu. If the player is named the next day's catcher, the catching and performance staff can revise timing and optional work. If field access disappears, record the substitution and what baseball-specific exposure it did not reproduce. A gym session can support physical preparation without pretending to replace a reactive fielding or baserunning task.

End the week by reviewing completed work, not just planned work. The ledger should make missed opportunities visible so the next week is informed rather than reactive. The most useful reserve plan is both ready to run and easy to revise: the athlete knows today's purpose, the staff knows who can change it, and everyone can see why it changed.
